Although Voat is superior to Reddit in that there has not been a systemic attempt to banish certain topics from discussion, we still have a long way to go in making the place an open forum for ideas. Voat's growth has come in waves, generally fueled by the exile of certain communities on Reddit. These groups bring a lot of strong beliefs with them, and because Voat's default subs are virtually unmoderated, the discourse here has come to be dominated by (for lack of a better term) ideologues that neither seek nor are capable of reasoned discussion. Nor are they particularly tolerant of opinions that don't reflect their particular world-view (e.g. anti-black, anti-Jew, anti-immigration). Even in technology Voat skews so far towards Linux that almost any slightly pro-Windows or vaguely critical Linux post will inflame passions.

The result is almost any post that does not adhere to the group-think mentality immediately gets downvoated behold the threshold and will not be seen except by the most curious of users. The reality of downvoating opinions into obscurity replicates one of Reddit's flaws as it pertains to "free speech." It effectively stops people with moderate, rational opinions from posting because their contributions are immediately downvoated into obscurity by ideologues. The ultimate result is an echo-chamber, a self-affirming community that skews far-right and is no more pro "free speech" than reddit. Instead these mechanics have led Voat to become a conservative/nationalist/racist counter to reddit.

So although Voat has a lot of potential as safe harbor for "free speech" it has not (yet) built a structure that either values or encourages it. Voat is effectively a "mob-rules" type of site where posting anything (regardless of facts, reason, or civility) that deviates from the narrative embraced by the "hate groups" exiled from reddit is utterly futile as it is effectively rendered invisible.
